notes.definition: Culturing microorganisms means growing them in a nutrient broth or on an agar gel plate. Bacteria multiply by simple cell division (binary fission), and uncontaminated cultures, prepared using aseptic technique, are needed to investigate the effect of chemicals such as disinfectants and antibiotics.
explanation: Bacteria multiply by simple cell division, called binary fission: one bacterial cell splits into two. If they have enough nutrients and a suitable temperature, bacteria can divide as often as once every 20 minutes. Because the number doubles with every division, a population can become enormous in just a few hours. Bacteria can be grown in the laboratory in a nutrient broth solution (a liquid containing the nutrients they need) or as colonies on an agar gel plate. Each colony is a visible mass of bacteria that has grown from a single cell.

To investigate the effect of chemicals such as disinfectants, antiseptics and antibiotics, scientists need uncontaminated cultures. A culture contaminated with other microorganisms would give unreliable results, because you could not tell which microorganism was being affected, and contaminating microorganisms could include pathogens that cause disease. Uncontaminated cultures are prepared using aseptic technique, a set of steps that stop unwanted microorganisms getting in.

The steps of aseptic technique each have a reason. Petri dishes and culture media (such as agar) must be sterilised before use, for example in an autoclave, to kill any microorganisms already present. Inoculating loops used to transfer microorganisms must be sterilised by passing them through a flame until red hot, to kill any microorganisms on them; the loop is allowed to cool before use so it does not kill the bacteria being transferred. The lid of the Petri dish is secured with adhesive tape to stop microorganisms from the air getting in. It is not sealed all the way round, so oxygen can still get in and harmful anaerobic bacteria do not grow.

The Petri dish is stored upside down, so that drops of condensation do not fall onto the agar surface and disturb the colonies. In school laboratories, cultures should generally be incubated at 25 °C. This reduces the chance of growing pathogens that could be harmful to humans, which grow best at around body temperature (37 °C). Lids should only be lifted slightly when transferring bacteria, and work is often done near a lit Bunsen burner, as the rising hot air carries microorganisms away from the plate.

In required practical 2, paper discs soaked in different antiseptics or antibiotics are placed on an agar plate spread with bacteria. After incubation, a clear zone (zone of inhibition) forms around each disc where the bacteria have been killed or their growth stopped. The bigger the clear zone, the more effective the chemical. To compare zones, measure the diameter, halve it to get the radius and calculate the area using πr². A disc soaked in sterile water is used as a control.
keyFacts: Bacteria multiply by simple cell division (binary fission).
Bacteria can divide as often as once every 20 minutes if they have enough nutrients and a suitable temperature.
Bacteria can be grown in a nutrient broth solution or as colonies on an agar gel plate.
Uncontaminated cultures are needed to investigate the effect of disinfectants and antibiotics.
Petri dishes and culture media are sterilised before use to kill unwanted microorganisms.
Inoculating loops are sterilised by passing them through a flame.
The Petri dish lid is secured with adhesive tape and the dish is stored upside down.
In school laboratories, cultures are incubated at 25 °C to reduce the chance of growing human pathogens.
Area of a clear zone or colony = πr².
Number of bacteria = starting number × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of divisions (Higher tier).

keyTerms.definition: Simple cell division in which one bacterial cell splits into two.
A substance containing the nutrients microorganisms need to grow, such as nutrient broth or agar gel.
A visible group of bacteria on an agar plate, grown from a single bacterial cell.
Methods used to prevent contamination of a culture by unwanted microorganisms.
To kill all microorganisms on or in something, for example by heating in a flame or in an autoclave.
A wire loop used to transfer microorganisms onto a culture medium.
An area around an antiseptic or antibiotic disc where bacteria have been killed or have not grown.
The average time taken for a population of bacteria to divide once (double in number).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the Petri dish lid should be taped all the way round to seal it.
misconceptions.right: In fact the lid is held with a few strips of tape. Sealing it completely would stop oxygen getting in and could encourage harmful anaerobic bacteria to grow.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think cultures should be incubated at 37 °C so bacteria grow faster.
misconceptions.right: In fact school cultures are incubated at 25 °C. At 37 °C (body temperature) pathogens that are harmful to humans are more likely to grow.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the dish is stored upside down to stop the agar falling out.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is stored upside down so that condensation does not drip onto the agar surface and disturb the colonies.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that after 3 divisions there are 3 times as many bacteria.
misconceptions.right: In fact the number doubles each division, so after 3 divisions there are 2³ = 8 times as many bacteria.

realWorld: Hospital laboratories culture bacteria from a patient's sample and test them with antibiotic discs to find out which antibiotic will work best for that infection.
Food safety rules about cooling and refrigerating food exist because bacteria can double every 20 minutes at warm temperatures, quickly reaching harmful numbers.
Manufacturers test new disinfectants and antiseptic hand gels on bacterial cultures to show how effective they are before they are sold.
higherTier: Calculate the number of bacteria in a population after a certain time if given the mean division time: number of divisions n = time ÷ mean division time, then number of bacteria = starting number × 2ⁿ. Give the answer in standard form where appropriate.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic, including required practical 2, is in separate Biology (8461) only. It is not assessed in Combined Science Trilogy (8464).
examTips: AQA often asks you to 'explain why' for each aseptic step. Give the step and its reason, e.g. 'flame the loop to kill any microorganisms on it'.
To calculate the area of a clear zone, remember to halve the diameter to get the radius before using πr². Using the diameter gives an answer four times too big.
In population calculations, convert hours to minutes first, then divide by the division time to find the number of divisions. Then use 2ⁿ, not 2 × n.
Give the reason for 25 °C precisely: it reduces the likelihood of growing pathogens that are harmful to humans. Do not just say 'it is safer'.
In required practical 2, the control disc soaked in sterile water shows that any clear zone is caused by the antiseptic, not by the disc itself.
summary: Bacteria multiply by binary fission, as often as every 20 minutes.
Bacteria are grown in nutrient broth or on agar gel plates.
Aseptic technique prevents contamination: sterilise dishes, media and loops.
Tape the lid (not fully sealed), store upside down, incubate at 25 °C in school.
Clear zones around antiseptic discs show effectiveness: area = πr².
Higher tier: number of bacteria = starting number × 2ⁿ.

questions.question: How do bacteria multiply?
markScheme: 1 mark: simple cell division (binary fission)
questions.explanation: Bacteria split into two by binary fission. Meiosis and fertilisation are part of sexual reproduction in eukaryotes, and seeds are produced by plants.

questions.question: With enough nutrients and a suitable temperature, how often can bacteria divide?
markScheme: 1 mark: once every 20 minutes
questions.explanation: In ideal conditions bacteria can divide as often as once every 20 minutes, which is why populations grow so quickly.

questions.question: At what temperature should cultures of bacteria generally be incubated in a school laboratory?
markScheme: 1 mark: 25 °C
questions.explanation: 25 °C reduces the chance of growing human pathogens. 37 °C is body temperature, ideal for pathogens; 4 °C is fridge temperature, where growth is very slow; 100 °C would kill the bacteria.

questions.question: Which piece of equipment is used to transfer bacteria onto an agar plate?
markScheme: 1 mark: inoculating loop
questions.explanation: An inoculating loop is used to transfer microorganisms. The Bunsen burner is used to sterilise the loop, but it does not transfer the bacteria.

markScheme: 1 mark: to kill any microorganisms on the loop
questions.explanation: Flaming sterilises the loop so no unwanted microorganisms contaminate the culture. The loop is cooled before use, otherwise it would kill the bacteria being transferred.

questions.question: Why is a Petri dish containing a bacterial culture stored upside down?
options: To let more light reach the bacteria
To stop the agar from melting
To stop condensation dripping onto the agar surface and disturbing the colonies
So that more oxygen can reach the bacteria
markScheme: 1 mark: to stop condensation dripping onto the agar surface
questions.explanation: Water condenses on the lid. If the dish were the right way up, drops would fall onto the agar and spread or disturb the colonies.

questions.question: Why are cultures in school laboratories incubated at 25 °C rather than 37 °C?
options: It reduces the chance of growing pathogens that could be harmful to humans
markScheme: 1 mark: it reduces the chance of growing pathogens that could be harmful to humans
questions.explanation: Human pathogens grow best near body temperature, 37 °C. At 25 °C they are less likely to grow. 25 °C does not kill bacteria, and many bacteria grow well at 37 °C.

questions.question:
A student investigated the effect of three antiseptics on the growth of bacteria.
The student placed four paper discs on an agar plate spread with bacteria. Each disc was soaked in a different liquid.
Table 1 shows the results.
Which disc contained the most effective antiseptic?

headers: Diameter of clear zone in mm

markScheme: 1 mark: B
questions.explanation: The largest clear zone (14 mm, disc B) shows where most bacteria were killed or stopped growing, so B is most effective. C is the control with no antiseptic, so no clear zone forms.

questions.question:
A single bacterium divides once every 20 minutes.
How many bacteria will there be after 2 hours?
markScheme: 1 mark: 64
questions.explanation: 2 hours = 120 minutes, so there are 120 ÷ 20 = 6 divisions. Number = 2⁶ = 64. 12 comes from 2 × 6 (doubling wrongly treated as adding) and 32 is 2⁵, one division too few.

The radius of the clear zone is 7 mm.
Calculate the area of the clear zone.
Use the equation: area = πr²
Use π = 3.14 or the π button on your calculator.

questions.explanation: Halve the diameter to get the radius: 6 mm. Area = π × 36 = 113.1 mm², which is 113 mm² to 3 significant figures. Using the diameter by mistake gives 452 mm².

questions.question:
A single bacterium has a mean division time of 20 minutes.
Calculate the number of bacteria present after 4 hours.
markScheme: 1 mark: number of divisions = 240 ÷ 20 = 12
questions.explanation: 4 hours = 240 minutes, giving 12 divisions. The number doubles each time: 1 × 2¹² = 4096.

questions.question:
A culture starts with 500 bacteria. The mean division time is 30 minutes.
Calculate the number of bacteria in the culture after 5 hours.
Give your answer in standard form. (Enter the full number, e.g. 5.12e5.)
markScheme: 1 mark: number of divisions = 300 ÷ 30 = 10
questions.explanation: 5 hours = 300 minutes, so there are 10 divisions. 2¹⁰ = 1024, and 500 × 1024 = 512 000, which is 5.12 × 10⁵ in standard form.

questions.question:
A single bacterium divides once every 20 minutes.
Calculate the number of bacteria after 8 hours.
Give your answer in standard form to 3 significant figures. (Enter the number, e.g. 1.68e7.)
markScheme: 1 mark: 8 hours = 480 minutes; 480 ÷ 20 = 24 divisions
questions.explanation: There are 24 divisions in 8 hours, so the number is 2²⁴ = 16 777 216, which is 1.68 × 10⁷ to 3 significant figures. This shows how quickly bacteria can reach huge numbers.

questions.question:
Bacteria in a culture divide once every 20 minutes.
Calculate how many times the bacteria will divide in 3 hours.
markScheme: 1 mark: 9
questions.explanation: 3 hours = 180 minutes. 180 ÷ 20 = 9 divisions.

questions.question:
A student measured the diameter of the clear zone around two antiseptics, X and Y.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate how much larger the area of the clear zone around X is than the area of the clear zone around Y.
Use the equation: area = πr²
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

headers: Diameter of clear zone in mm

markScheme: 1 mark: area X = π × 8² = 201 mm²
1 mark: area Y = π × 5² = 78.5 mm²
1 mark: difference = 123 mm² (accept 122 to 123)
questions.explanation: Radii are 8 mm and 5 mm. Areas: π × 64 = 201.1 mm² and π × 25 = 78.5 mm². Difference = 122.5 mm², which is 123 mm² to 3 significant figures (π × 39).

questions.question: Name two types of culture medium that bacteria can be grown in or on.
markScheme: 1 mark: nutrient broth (solution)
1 mark: agar gel (plate)
questions.explanation: Bacteria can grow in a liquid nutrient broth or as colonies on the surface of an agar gel plate.

questions.question: Explain why Petri dishes and culture media must be sterilised before use.
markScheme: 1 mark: to kill any microorganisms (already present)
1 mark: so the culture is not contaminated / only the bacteria being studied grow
questions.explanation: Unwanted microorganisms on the dish or in the agar would grow alongside the culture, contaminating it and possibly including pathogens.

acceptedAnswers: stop microorganisms from the air getting in
markScheme: 1 mark: tape stops microorganisms from the air getting in / contaminating the culture (or stops the lid being opened)
1 mark: not fully sealed so oxygen can get in / to prevent growth of (harmful) anaerobic bacteria
questions.explanation: Taping stops contamination from the air. Leaving gaps lets oxygen in, which discourages anaerobic bacteria, some of which are dangerous pathogens.

questions.question: Explain why an uncontaminated culture is needed when investigating the effect of an antibiotic on a type of bacterium.
acceptedAnswers: results only show effect on that bacterium
markScheme: 1 mark: other microorganisms might respond differently to the antibiotic / could grow in the clear zone
1 mark: so the results would not be valid / you could not tell the effect on the bacterium being studied
questions.explanation: If other microorganisms were present, any growth or clear zones could be due to them, so you could not draw valid conclusions about the bacterium being tested.

questions.question:
A student investigates the effect of different antiseptics on the growth of bacteria.
Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
markScheme: 1 mark: independent variable: type of antiseptic
1 mark: dependent variable: area (or diameter) of the clear zone
questions.explanation: The variable the student changes is the antiseptic. The variable measured is the size of the clear zone, best compared as an area using πr².

questions.question: Give three control variables in an investigation comparing the effect of different antibiotics on bacterial growth.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any three from: type of bacteria; volume / concentration of bacterial culture; size of paper disc; concentration of antibiotic; time discs are soaked; type / depth of agar; incubation temperature; incubation time
questions.explanation: Keeping these the same means any difference in clear zone size is caused only by the type of antibiotic, making it a fair test.

questions.question:
A student investigated the effect of three antiseptics on the growth of bacteria.
Figure 1 shows the agar plate after incubation.
One paper disc was soaked in sterile water instead of an antiseptic.

questions.question: What is meant by a bacterial colony on an agar plate?
acceptedAnswers: group of bacteria from a single bacterium
markScheme: 1 mark: a (visible) group / mass of bacteria grown from a single bacterium
questions.explanation: A single bacterium on the agar divides many times. Eventually the millions of bacteria form a spot that can be seen with the naked eye: a colony.

questions.question: A student calculates that one bacterium dividing every 20 minutes would produce over 4.7 × 10²¹ bacteria in 24 hours. Suggest two reasons why the real number would be much smaller.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: nutrients run out; toxic waste products build up; lack of space; oxygen runs out; temperature not always suitable; some bacteria die
questions.explanation: Bacteria only divide every 20 minutes when they have enough nutrients and a suitable temperature. As the population grows, nutrients are used up and waste builds up, so division slows and cells die.

questions.question: Describe how to prepare an uncontaminated culture of bacteria on an agar plate using aseptic technique. Explain the reason for each step.
markScheme: Indicative content:
sterilise Petri dishes and agar before use (e.g. autoclave) to kill microorganisms already present
pass the inoculating loop through a flame until red hot to kill microorganisms on it
let the loop cool before use so it does not kill the bacteria being transferred
lift the Petri dish lid only slightly / work near a Bunsen flame to reduce microorganisms from the air entering
transfer bacteria with the loop and spread over the agar
secure the lid with adhesive tape to stop microorganisms from the air getting in
do not seal completely, so oxygen can enter and harmful anaerobic bacteria do not grow
store the dish upside down so condensation does not drip onto the agar
incubate at 25 °C to reduce the likelihood of growing pathogens harmful to humans
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a logical sequence of aseptic steps, each with a correct reason.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): several correct steps with some reasons given.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two steps with little or no explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Each aseptic step has a matching reason, and AQA expects both. The four core steps in the specification are: sterilise dishes and media, flame the loop, tape the lid and store upside down, and incubate at 25 °C.

questions.question:
A student wants to compare how well three antibiotics stop bacteria growing. She places paper discs soaked in each antibiotic on an agar plate spread with bacteria and incubates it.
Describe how she should process her results to compare the antibiotics, and how she would decide which antibiotic is most effective.
markScheme: Indicative content:
measure the diameter of the clear zone around each disc with a ruler
measure across more than one direction and calculate a mean diameter
radius = diameter ÷ 2
area of clear zone = πr²
compare areas: the largest clear zone shows the most effective antibiotic
compare with the control disc (no clear zone)
repeat the experiment and calculate mean areas to check repeatability
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description including calculating area using πr² and correctly identifying that the largest area shows the most effective antibiotic.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): measures clear zone or states largest zone is best, without calculation detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Measuring diameter, halving it and using πr² turns each clear zone into an area that can be compared fairly. The largest area shows the most effective antibiotic, and repeats improve confidence in the result.
